documents.name: interview02-english-excerpts.txt
documents.text:
So, moving on to the method, we worked on the printed text — on two printed editions, let us say.

Sometimes there are errors that need to be corrected in the Latin text, or things that are not understood. Sometimes there are gaps because something was lost during printing, in the passage from manuscript to print, and so the text has to be critically restored with the help of two printed editions.

This is [something new] compared with when I began this kind of research. Fifteen years ago I would of course have had to go to the library. Now one edition has been digitised by Google Books, while for the 1502 edition we used the digitised print from the Bavarian State Library in Munich, which is an exceptional repository of early printed books. Seventy per cent of what we look for among incunabula, late-fifteenth-century printed books and sixteenth-century editions can be found there.

All this is to establish a critical text and a stemma codicum that helps me understand its transmission: where the text originated, how it spread, and what kinds of corruption then arose in that transmission.

As regards the edition, we first built a website that is open to everyone, for public engagement, so to speak. There is also a password-protected section that we use for our work.

documents.name: interview04-english-excerpts.txt
documents.text:
Generally speaking, the object of my studies — given the nature of my discipline — is manuscript sources, usually from the medieval and/or Renaissance period. Manuscripts is a broad term, and I use it broadly: it can mean codices, manuscript books, or handwritten documents. These can of course be very different, with different materials and supports: often parchment, but also paper. They are always manuscript sources. My work is, as it were, to elucidate these sources and make them accessible, through a critical edition or through studies, to people working in history, philology, literature and so on.

Certainly, however, the field is also opening up with great interest — sometimes through experimental research — to the possibility of digital editions. Digital editions are undoubtedly one of the new frontiers of our field.

I would add that I work in palaeography and diplomatics. These are two very broad disciplines: connected, but also different. We have always had two strands: a more philological one, traditionally working on codices and books, and a more historical one, working on documents. The Bologna school has tended towards the documentary and diplomatic tradition — the study and editing of documentary sources. I try to carry on that tradition because that is how I was trained, but I am also open to the more philological side. Both interest me, so in practice I move between the two.

method_map.name: Qualitative Content Analysis
method_map.note: Content analysis is a complete method. It is not a compulsory preliminary stage for TA or Comparative QCA.

steps.title: Declare unit and approach
steps.detail: Document what is analysed and the chosen content analysis approach.

steps.title: Select meaning units
steps.detail: Identify relevant passages while retaining their surrounding context.

steps.title: Condense when appropriate
steps.detail: Shorten meaning units only when this fits the analytic design.

steps.title: Code and review categories
steps.detail: Compare codes and refine categories with explicit analytic decisions.

steps.title: Interpret in context
steps.detail: Consider meaning and abstraction; themes are optional, design-dependent.

steps.title: Write with evidence
steps.detail: Connect categories, interpretation and source quotations in the report.

references.title: Graneheim and Lundman (2004) · concepts and procedures

draft.title: Bologna coding evidence report
draft.research_question: How are research materials described in this saved Bologna coding record?
draft.case_unit: This English teaching subset contains selected translated passages from three public Bologna interviews. The Notebook covers all excerpts selected from interview02.txt, not the full original interview.
draft.analysis_unit: An existing quotation and its saved code path, read in the context of the full source document.
draft.method_notes: This is a worked software example using translated Bologna excerpts and source-linked teaching associations. Translated offsets refer to the English teaching documents, not the Italian originals. This is not a new empirical analysis. Table labels retain the saved ancestry. Method steps show the workflow; unchecked review stages remain unconfirmed.
draft.reflexivity: The short illustrative narrative was prepared for the QT demonstration. It is not an independently validated analysis of this corpus.
draft.quality_notes: Quoted characters and code identities were checked against the saved source. All five figures use only this three-document translated teaching subset and the unchanged counting rules.
draft.narrative:
The selected passages describe different forms of research material. Their saved paths place these distinctions inside the materials group. Read the exact quotations before judging how well each code fits. [E:3f029191a6885f0e9fdef6174d572dff] [E:9ebf2d198c4b5376b175ec0e8a4af023] [E:385e5468906559869404264689236561]
The five figures summarize all existing codings across the corpus. They support checking the record; they do not substitute for interpretation of the interviews.
draft.counterexamples: Only selected material-related passages are interpreted here. Contrasting perspectives across the other interviews require further contextual reading.
draft.limitations: This small writing example does not establish a complete analysis or saturation. Counts describe saved coding activity rather than importance or prevalence among people.
draft.disclosure: Public Bologna CC0 data only. No private interviews or model calls were used. Editing the downloaded Word documents does not change the QT project.
